Christian Parker's job as Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator is safe for now, but he will no longer be calling the plays, head coach Brian Schottenheimer said on Wednesday.

Mike Pettine, who was added last month as a senior defensive assistant to support Parker, will have play-calling responsibilities going forward.

"A different perspective [will be] good for us," Schottenheimer said. "Play-calling is a very collaborative thing."

The decision comes after another poor showing by the Dallas defense during Sunday's 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. After the game, head coach Brian Schottenheimer didn't exactly show support for the 34-year-old Parker, who was hired in the offseason after two seasons on Nick Sirianni's staff with the Philadelphia Eagles.

"At the end of the day, we tackled like s**t in the second half," Scottenheimer said after the 49ers recorded 584 yards of offense, the most the Cowboys have allowed at home in franchise history.

Longtime ESPN analyst and former NFL linebacker Tom Jackson has died. He was 75.

Jackson was a fixture on ESPN's NFL coverage after his playing career ended in 1986. He joined the network in 1987 and worked alongside Chris Berman for nearly 30 years until his retirement in 2016.

Berman eulogized his friend and colleague during ESPN's "Sunday NFL Countdown," expressing his shock after seeing Jackson weeks ago at the network's studios in Bristol, Connecticut and talking to him last week.

Jackson died on Friday, according to Berman. His family informed ESPN of his death soon thereafter.

"Sunday Night Football" just got a little more interesting.

The Patriots may have the most urgent need after Drake Maye suffered a fractured fibula in Week 10, though there's hope he could return by the end of the season.

Baker Mayfield is expected to start at quarterback for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers versus the Detroit Lions on Sunday, despite being listed as questionable on the injury report.

However, the nine-year veteran is struggling with plantar fascitis in his foot, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reports. Mayfield is determined to continue playing through the injury, which has required him to wear a walking boot during the Bucs' bye week.

Mayfield is also recovering from a right thumb injury that sidelined him for Tampa Bay's past three games. However, coach Todd Bowles said the QB looked good in Friday's practice in anticipation of playing on Sunday.

text:
The Indianapolis Colts said goodbye to two of their top receivers at this year's NFL trade deadline, and now it appears they plan to exercise great caution regarding the return of their most accomplished wideout.

Sources told NFL Network that the Colts are planning for Alec Pierce to be fully healthy for 2027, rebuffing his efforts to return with a few games left this season.

Despite his attempts, Pierce's season is almost certainly over, according to sources.

Considering the Colts traded away four key players prior to the deadline and released starting quarterback Daniel Jones on Friday, shelving Pierce until next season is prudent.

With their 3-8 record, this makes the most sense from an organizational standpoint -- especially considering Indianapolis' long-term investment of $114 million in Pierce.

Sources said Pierce has been working tirelessly in his rehab from his heel injury, which he suffered when he fought his way onto the field and came back before he was fully ready. The Colts' goal is to avoid a similar situation next year, which is why the team is insisting that his 2026 season is over.

Pierce aggravated his surgically repaired heel in late September and had been hoping to return to the field. Yet the Colts provided little clarity in the past few weeks about his timetable.

text:
While the Los Angeles Rams try to make the most of a 2026 campaign that began with astronomical expectations, wide receiver Puka Nacua is already working toward 2027. He had MCL surgery on Tuesday, and his recovery timeline is considered to be four to five months, ESPN's Adam Schefter reported on Saturday night.

Based on that reported prognosis, the 25-year-old Nacua will miss the remainder of the regular season and the playoffs.

The two-time All-Pro wideout received recommendations from three doctors to undergo the procedure, per ESPN's latest report, which noted that team doctor Neal ElAttrache performed the operation.

When the NFL announced this week that it was suspending Nacua three games for violating the league's personal conduct policy, it reportedly wasn't aware that he had already had surgery.

The Rams placed Nacua on injured reserve with knee and turf toe injuries on Nov. 12, a week before the NFL imposed its suspension. Like any player who lands on IR, Nacua had to sit out four games before he could return. By the time the suspension was announced, the length of that ban and his remaining time on IR were aligned.

While that situation understandably turned heads, it's worth noting that Nacua isn't the first player to serve a suspension while on IR.

The last year has been a head-scratching one for Nacua, who's among the best wide receivers in the sport but has run into off-field trouble.

This past offseason, news broke that a woman was suing Nacua. She alleged that, on Dec. 31, 2025, he made an antisemitic statement and later bit her on the shoulder. Nacua's attorney denied the woman's claim that he made such a comment and downplayed the biting as "horseplay."

Nacua voluntarily entered a holistic care facility in March to focus on his personal growth. He reflected on that experience in May.

In seven games this season, Nacua — the league's 2025 receptions leader — piled up 70 catches for 715 yards and 4 touchdowns. He also scored on the ground once for a 6-4 Rams team that's hardly had the start it envisioned this fall.

Nacua's injuries occurred on the final offensive snap of L.A.'s Week 9 win over the Washington Commanders. He's in the last year of his rookie contract.

text:
Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce shared his thoughts on what some fans thought was a "dirty" hit that left him briefly injured against the Atlanta Falcons last week, and the NFL has now had its final say on the play.

Kelce was hurt after Atlanta Falcons safety DeMarcco Hellams tackled him low, aggravating an already injured ankle. There was some speculation that Hellams may have intentionally tried to injure Kelce, and the Chiefs tight end would not say one way or the other.

But the league decided on Saturday that Hellams did not run afoul of any rules with the hit.

NFL Decides Against Fine for Falcons Player

The NFL announced fines for all Week 10 games on Saturday, with nothing listed for the Falcons in their loss to the Chiefs last week.

Kelce had addressed the hit on his "New Heights" podcast this week, answering a question from a fan who called the hit "dirty."

"I don't know if that was the case; the way he tackled me… and I just got caught in a bad position," Kelce replied. "You know, that's football. And on the flip side, you know, if it was a quote-unquote intentional, you know, extra grab and turn of the ankle, you know, it's just part of it."

Kelce agreed that the play did not warrant a flag, as Hellams made a legal hit, but said it did leave him hurt. The Chiefs tight end was in visible pain and briefly left the game, but was able to return.

"I don't think it was, you know, crazy enough for it to get a flag or it to be a fine or anything like that," Kelce said. "Obviously, in the moment, I thought it was, because it hurt like hell."

Chiefs Have Chance to Make Up Ground

The Chiefs have turned their attention to Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals, where they will face a well-traveled veteran quarterback. The Cardinals ruled out Carson Beck, handing the ball instead to Josh Johnson.

Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur shared praise for the 40-year-old.

"You've got to have a baseline talent level, which clearly half the league has felt like [Johnson] has," LaFleur said. "He is incredible in the quarterback room. He's incredible for the starter. He's incredible for young quarterbacks in terms of just the way he sees the game, his energy, his positivity, how he keeps it real. He's mature, and he can still sling it. He's been in this league. It's not like he was just on the street."

Alec Pierce's season appears to be over.

NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Sunday the Indianapolis Colts are likely to shut down the wide receiver, who has appeared in just two games in 2026. Pierce has been sidelined since mid-September because of a heel injury.

This decision comes days after Indianapolis waived quarterback Daniel Jones.

The Colts hit the reset button weeks ago by firing general manager Chris Ballard and then trading Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. More trades followed. Now, Jones is on the way out, only months after he signed a two-year, $88 million contract.

When the organization has given up on the season, there isn't much sense in having Pierce risk another injury setback given that exact situation unfolded once already. He had offseason surgery and "came back before he was fully ready," in the words of Rapoport.

The Colts have Pierce signed for three more seasons, and his salary cap hit begins climbing north of $30 million in 2027. His and the Colts' focus should be on doing everything they can to have him rebound next year.

In the meantime, the state of Indy's passing game will be dire over the final six games. Anthony Richardson Sr. is back as the starting quarterback, and Laquon Treadwell, Deion Burks and Anthony Gould are his best aerial targets.

text:
Baker Mayfield is dealing with a painful case of plantar fasciitis, sources told NFL Network, an injury that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback is determined to play through.

Mayfield is officially listed as questionable for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions, but sources told NFL Network that the two-time Pro Bowler will play.

Bucs coach Todd Bowles told reporters Mayfield had a good day Friday, indicating he's likely the starter against Detroit.

"We'll see how his leg feels the next two days," Bowles said, but he's trending in the right direction."

The Bucs practiced in their indoor facility on Friday with artificial turf -- with the idea being to test Mayfield's foot. Mayfield passed that test and is good to go Sunday.

Mayfield suffered the injury against the Chicago Bears in Week 9 and worked around the clock to rehab during the bye, often wearing a walking boot. The pain comes mostly in the arch and under his heel, sources say, and based on the nature of the injury, it will likely linger.

Mayfield's injury is considered a strain -- not a sprain -- because it affects his fascia, which can be a challenge specifically for quarterbacks.

Historically, Drew Brees once played through this injury while Peyton Manning was not able to -- both with varying degrees of the injury.

For Mayfield, who wants to play through everything, the risk is not in performance but in aggravating the injury and making it linger all season.

Mayfield also is on the injury report as he recovers from his dislocated thumb on his throwing hand that won't fully heal until he gives it the proper rest. He previously missed three games with the thumb injury.

Mayfield said he "felt good" in Thursday's practice and, when asked what he needs to do to be confident that he can play Sunday, said he just has to continue what he's been doing since the Bears game.

"Doing everything I can to get all the treatment and rehab possible and prepare like a professional," he said. "So, for me ... if I continue that, I imagine being able to play."

Mayfield said he would have "no shame" if it comes to the point he has to admit that rookie Jalon Daniels gives the Buccaneers a better chance to win at Detroit.

Daniels started three games for the Buccaneers earlier this season when Mayfield was sidelined by a dislocated thumb.

Mayfield has thrown for 922 yards, completing 60.6% of his pass attempts, with three touchdowns and four interceptions this season. Daniels has thrown for 501 yards, completing 61.2% of his attempts, with three touchdowns and five interceptions.

A lot of pundits and fans questioned the Denver Broncos' move to select tight end Caleb Lohner in the seventh round of the 2025 NFL draft, and after he didn't see action last fall, the tight end was kept on the short-term injured reserve list to begin the season.

The Broncos opened the 21-day window for Lohner to return to action on Wednesday, and he practiced for the first time all year after missing minicamp, OTAs, and all of training camp following a lower-body procedure in early June. Coach Sean Payton spoke about Lohner's long road to recovery, and potential action in his post-practice remarks on Wednesday.

"It’s good to get him out here," Payton said to the Denver media. "He’s worked his tail off. Today was his first practice. He was making a lot of strides, and that setback was unfortunate, but he has that spirit, that will. You never felt like he lost interest. So it was good to see him moving around."

Lohner is an interesting player, simply because of his background in basketball, and his surprising path to being a seventh-round pick. Prior to 2024, Lohner mostly made his name as a college basketball player at BYU, Utah and Baylor. Lohner spent all of 2025 on Denver's practice squad, developing into a football player.

At May's rookie minicamp, Lohner appeared as an eligible first-year player, impressing Payton and other coaches with his development.

"He looks entirely different in this camp," Payton said of Lohner at the time. "One year into the program, and how he’s moving, what he’s doing, everything looks entirely different. That learning curve and growth curve was greater for someone who had far less experience, maybe, than others, if that makes sense. It’s entirely noticeable, and he’s in great shape. You see his athleticism."

If Lohner is activated, it will mark his first-ever NFL action. The Broncos could be waiting to see if he can be a receiving threat in the offense, as several of their in-house tight ends are set to hit free agency at the end of 2026, including Evan Engram and Nate Adkins.

In the meantime, Lohner is in a waiting game to see if he'll be activated, or revert to season-ending injured reserve at some point in the next 20 days.

text:
PITTSBURGH -- Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf has never had a season like this.

A career-worst 7% drop rate. Catching a career-low 49.3% of his targets. Averaging, you guessed it, a career-low 48 yards per game and 12.3 yards per reception.

Amid the lows, though, the 28-year-old still made a handful of special plays. There was the 22-yard touchdown reception late in the loss to the Cincinnati Bengals and the 32-yard catch-and-run earlier in the game. There was also the 115-yard game against the Cleveland Browns in Week 4 and the 11-catch outing in the overtime win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 6.

"This is the first time for real," Metcalf said of his struggles Thursday. "But I don't look at it as inconsistency. It's just new territory that I got to maneuver through. ... I've just got to block out the bulls--- y'all be talking about, basically."

Metcalf, who was acquired by the historically conservative organization in a blockbuster deal that included a second-round pick on the eve of 2025 free agency, was supposed to be a focal point of the offense. Instead, the mercurial wide receiver has been defined more by volatility than reliability, and this season, his 49.3% catch rate is second worst in the league out of 133 qualified players, per ESPN Research.

His teammates, though, have remained vocal in their support of him, and the coaching staff has shouldered some of the blame, saying it has to scheme up better opportunities for Metcalf.

"He's been up and down this season, and he's the first to admit that," tight end Pat Freiermuth said. "We need consistency out of him, but I've never worried about if his mind's in the right place or if he's willing to go out there and play. I think that obviously he's had some struggles, but him going out there -- and if you look at his effort on the run game or just downfield blocking, he doesn't let his situation impact his ability to get other guys open.

"That's something that you can appreciate as a teammate and as a guy, it tells a lot about his character, but we're with him till the end. He's going to get this figured out. We've got a lot of trust in DK and a lot of belief in him."

Compounding Metcalf's struggles this season has been the rash of wide receiver injuries.

But this week, Metcalf and the passing game, which averaged just 158.7 yards in the past three games, are poised to get a boost with the return of receivers Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr. Though neither has been officially activated from injured reserve, each is listed as questionable for Sunday's game in Philadelphia (1 p.m. ET, CBS) after fully participating in practices Thursday and Friday.

"Instead of having four receivers up, we'll probably have five or six," Metcalf said of the pair's impact. "So I mean a lot more rotation, a lot of fresh bodies. Just watching them out there at practice these past couple days, they look fresh, they look ready to go to me."

Both Pittman and Wilson were expected to be complementary players in the Steelers' offense this season, part of the core group of receivers along with rookie Germie Bernard and Metcalf.

But the Steelers have had their complete set of receivers for only three games this season, and Pittman was managing the foot injury that eventually landed him on injured reserve in two of those outings.

Pittman, acquired for a sixth-round pick earlier this year, hasn't contributed the way the Steelers envisioned. Added for his versatility and consistent production in Indianapolis, the veteran has just seven catches for 89 yards in three games this season.

"Just being out there when I'm needed, just those opportunities out there, just create plays, throw some nice blocks and play hard, just bring that physicality and just someone that the guys can depend on and just be there for any situation," Pittman said when asked how he can make a difference. "If it's a run-the-ball type game, hey, I'm in there to block safeties and linebackers, and if it's a pass game, then great. Get out there and let's catch some passes."

Pittman also added that his inclusion Sunday will depend on his ability to still move effectively on his foot.

"I don't want to go out there and hurt this team because I can't do something that I should be able to do," he said.

Wilson, meanwhile, was starting to become a dependable deep threat for quarterback Aaron Rodgers when he dislocated one finger and fractured another against the Colts in Week 5. Prior to the injury, he had six targets in each of the first four games and had a touchdown in back-to-back games for the first time in his three-year pro career.

"Obviously it's not ideal, but it's all part of the plan," Wilson said. "It's all part of the process. There's ups and downs. So as long as you just keep going forward, great things are going to happen."

And while Pittman and Wilson have the potential to give the offense its biggest boost, the Steelers could get help from an unexpected contributor: practice squad receiver Max Hurleman. A week ago, Rodgers brought up Hurleman's name unprompted as someone who could contribute, and earlier this week, he advocated for the 5-foot-11 former undrafted free agent, who spent three years of his collegiate career at Colgate, to make plays on special teams.

Like Wilson and Pittman, Hurleman was also sidelined with an undisclosed injury and rejoined the team earlier this week.

"Yeah, 'White Chocolate' is going to give y'all some plays, especially when he's out there on the field," Metcalf said last week, giving Hurleman a spur-of-the-moment nickname. "So I'm looking forward to him making his debut. He's been making plays ever since his rookie year last year, so definitely looking forward to him being out there."

Puka Nacua's recovery time from MCL surgery is considered to be four to five months, sources told ESPN on Saturday, meaning the Los Angeles Rams star wide receiver will miss the rest of this season, including the playoffs.

Sources told ESPN that three doctors recommended that Nacua undergo the procedure, which is expected to have him healthy for the 2027 campaign.

Nacua's right knee checked out clean aside from the MCL, according to a source. The operation was performed by team doctor Neal ElAttrache, a source told ESPN.

Rams coach Sean McVay said Friday that Nacua, who is serving a three-game suspension while on injured reserve, will likely miss at least the rest of the regular season after undergoing surgery Tuesday.

McVay added that the possibility of Nacua returning for the postseason was a scenario that the Rams "haven't thought about."

The NFL was unaware that Nacua had already undergone surgery when it imposed its suspension, a source told ESPN on Friday.

In seven games this season, Nacua had 70 catches for 715 yards and four touchdowns. The two-time Pro Bowler suffered the knee injury, along with a turf toe injury, on the Rams' final offensive snap of their Week 9 victory over the Washington Commanders and was placed on IR on Nov. 12.

Nacua, 25, is playing on the final year of his rookie deal and is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent this offseason.

The Washington Commanders got some bad news at the end of Friday's practice. Starting cornerback Amik Robertson suffered an ankle injury on the last day of practice. He did not practice on Saturday and the Commanders listed him as questionable on the final injury report for Monday night's game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Losing Robertson would be significant. He's been Washington's best and most consistent defensive back. His competitiveness sets the tone for the entire team. According to head coach Dan Quinn, Robertson could be a game-time decision on Monday.

"So, yeah, [Amik's injury] on the last play of the day [Friday], so it was sore today, so we held [him] out. I'll monitor over the next, you know, 48 hours," Quinn said.

In some good news, no players were ruled out for Monday night's game. However, three others were listed as questionable:

CB Amik Robertson: ankle

RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt: groin

RB Rachaad White: heel

C Lucas Patrick: concussion

Croskey-Merritt had his 21-day window opened last week. Quinn indicated on Saturday that things were trending positively for Washington's starting running back to return on Monday.

White has handled the bulk of running back duties while Croskey-Merritt is out, but Quinn seemed to indicate that he believed White could play against the Bengals.

Finally, Patrick is listed as questionable, but practiced fully on Saturday and Quinn said he'd be back in the starting lineup. He suffered a concussion two weeks ago against the Rams and missed last week's win over the Giants. Former starter Nick Allegretti played well in Patrick's absence.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – After a four-game absence, Green Bay Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin returned to practice on Saturday and intends to play against the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday night.

“I’ve been through a lot of things in my life, but I will say it was definitely one of the harder moments, just not being able to be out there with the guys,” Franklin said after practice. “It’s just a position I’m really not used to, but God makes no mistakes and I’ve been prayed up and I’ve been working my ass off to get back on the field. So, now we’re here.”

Franklin suffered a fractured shin during the Thursday practice before the Week 7 game at the Lions.

What happened?

“It was truly just a freak accident,” he explained. “Something that I really couldn’t even describe. I shoot the gap clean, somebody just kind of kneed me in a weird way. I’m thinking it’s just dead leg. I actually finished practice. I practiced two more periods on a broken leg. And then once I got the X-ray and it was broke, I was looking like, I almost couldn’t believe it. It just looked fake.

“The only thing that was going through my mind was, ‘Damn, I can’t practice tomorrow?’ It’s been a journey but I’m glad we were able to push through. Thank God for keeping my head down and really been leaning on my family. I’m just glad to be back.”

He practiced with a broken leg?

“I feel like there’s a difference between being hurt and being injured,” he said. “I’m just so used to being hurt so I just put it in that category immediately until I couldn’t walk the next day. Then I said, ‘Oh, damn, I might be injured.’ But thank God we were able to work through it.”

Franklin stayed active behind the scenes with Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'Ron Hopper. While he said there is only so much he could do without being on the field, his leadership the past few weeks was appreciated.

“The leadership is obviously the first thing that sticks out,” position coach Sam Siefkes said this week. “He’s been in the league for, what, eight years, so that part I think upticked with him being injured, which was cool to see. He was coaching the guys who were playing in Duff and Hopp and kind of being another person that can help them on the sideline as well as the meeting room.

“That part I give him a lot of credit for, because it’s tough when you’re in those situations, especially when he’s only missed a game. It’s easy to kind of take a back seat and kind of feel sorry for yourself, but he didn’t do that one ounce. For him to be able to take even another step in his leadership role was an awesome thing for him to put forth.”

Franklin had been practically impervious to injury throughout his career. After being drafted by the Colts in 2018, he had missed only one game in his first eight seasons. He started 67 of a possible 68 games during the 2022 through 2025 seasons.

So, it was weird for Franklin to not be practicing and playing. And now he is in the unfamiliar position of having to work his way back from an injury.

“It’s been humbling a little bit,” he said. “I’m just so used to pushing through every single thing until something came up that I wasn’t meant to push through. Just leaning on the training staff, trusting my body, trusting myself, but also knowing that I got that other side of me, that other edge to push through what I need to.

“I feel like the staff did a great job, my team and everybody off the field did a great job of helping me get back, ready to play. Just looking forward to getting back out there with the guys.”

Franklin will practice again on Sunday and Monday to knock off some of the rust and reintegrate himself into one of the better defenses in the league. While he commended McDuffie and Hopper for holding down the fort without him, Franklin presumably will be back in full-time duty as a defensive captain against the Rams on what he called a holiday “made up” by the NFL to create another opportunity to put games on TV.

“I’ve played on Christmas but I don’t think I played Thanksgiving,” he said. “So, this is a new thing. I’m looking forward to it. Are they going to have turkey? It’s Thanksgiving Eve, though.”

Maybe there will be a turducken, he wondered.

“That’s what I need. Need that. Need that, for sure,” he said.

Franklin played in all 17 games in 2022, 2024 and 2025 with the Colts. That was his intention with the Packers, too. Instead, after missing four games, the max he can play is 13.

Unless the team makes it to the playoffs and makes a run.

“I genuinely believe everything happens for a reason,” Franklin said. “I had a close friend tell me that I came here to play 17; I just got to play 17 a different way. We missed four; that means we got to get the extra four. I’m just glad I’m back, ready to play.”

text:
Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson has received some welcome news following the devastating injury he suffered against the New England Patriots.

The NFL released its official Week 10 fines on Saturday, November 21, and Hutchinson was not among the players punished for their actions on the field.

That means Hutchinson has avoided a fine for his controversial sack of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye during Detroit’s 35-10 victory in Munich, Germany, on November 15.

The play injured Maye’s ankle and sparked accusations that Hutchinson had committed an illegal hip-drop tackle. Hutchinson subsequently suffered a season-ending torn ACL while celebrating the sack.

Although the NFL previously determined the tackle was legal, Saturday’s announcement confirms that Hutchinson was not financially penalized for the play.

NFL Makes Final Decision on Aidan Hutchinson’s Controversial Tackle

The controversy began when Hutchinson brought Maye to the ground from behind during the first quarter of Detroit’s win.

Maye’s ankle was caught underneath the defender during the tackle, forcing the Patriots quarterback out of the game. The play immediately generated debate over whether Hutchinson had violated the NFL’s prohibition against hip-drop tackles.

However, FOX rules analyst Mike Pereira explained during the broadcast that the tackle did not satisfy the requirements for an illegal hip drop.

The NFL subsequently agreed with Pereira’s interpretation.

According to NBC Sports’ Charean Williams, league officiating rules analyst Walt Anderson confirmed through a spokesman that Hutchinson did not swivel or unweight himself during the tackle, two elements required for the penalty.

No flag was thrown on the play.

Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel also defended Hutchinson following the game.

“However it happened, I don’t think it was anything intentional,” Vrabel said, according to NBC Sports.

Saturday’s NFL accountability report provides further confirmation that Hutchinson avoided discipline.

The league issued 21 fines for Week 10, including an $8,381 fine against New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Vernon Broughton for an illegal hip-drop tackle.

Detroit cornerback Rock Ya-Sin was also fined $11,941 for a facemask violation in the Patriots game.

Hutchinson’s name was absent from the list.

Aidan Hutchinson Faces Lengthy Recovery From Torn ACL

While Hutchinson avoided financial punishment, the circumstances surrounding the tackle delivered a devastating blow to Detroit’s defense.

After bringing Maye to the ground, Hutchinson jumped into the air as part of his sack celebration. His right knee buckled upon landing, leaving him in obvious pain.

He was eventually ruled out of the game, and further testing confirmed a torn ACL that will sideline him for the remainder of the season.

The injury adds another significant setback to Hutchinson’s NFL career. The former No. 2 overall pick previously suffered a gruesome broken leg during the 2024 season before returning to establish himself as one of Detroit’s most important defensive players.

Now the Lions must navigate the remainder of the 2026 campaign without their star pass rusher, beginning with their November 22 matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Detroit already has experience dealing with Hutchinson’s absence, but replacing his production and ability to disrupt opposing quarterbacks represents a considerable challenge for the defense.

At least one lingering question from his final appearance of the season has been answered.

Despite the controversy surrounding Maye’s injury, the NFL’s latest disciplinary report confirms Hutchinson will not face a fine for the tackle.

description:
Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson will not be fined for the tackle that injured New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye last Sunday, Front Office Sports' Mark Maske reported Saturday.
"Some had raised the possibility that it was a hip drop tackle," Maske reported.
Hutchinson sacked Maye on the Patriots' first drive of a 35-10 loss last weekend in Munich, Germany.
Hutchinson suffered a torn right ACL while celebrating the sack and is out for the season, per NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.
Fox Sports rules analyst Mike Pereira initially said during the Munich game broadcast Hutchinson's sack didn't qualify as a hip-drop tackle (h/t ESPN's Mike Reiss).
text:
Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson will not be fined for the tackle that injured New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye last Sunday, Front Office Sports' Mark Maske reported Saturday.

"Some had raised the possibility that it was a hip drop tackle," Maske reported. "But while it had some of the elements needed for such a tackle to be illegal (grab, swivel, unweight, fall on the ballcarrier's leg or legs), it was always highly debatable whether all the necessary elements were there."

Hutchinson sacked Maye on the Patriots' first drive of a 35-10 loss last weekend in Munich, Germany.

Maye suffered a fractured right fibula that won't require surgery but could keep him out "deep into the regular season, if he is able to return this year at all," ESPN's Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter reported.

Hutchinson suffered a torn right ACL while celebrating the sack and is out for the season, per NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

The NFL officially banned the hip-drop tackle ahead of the 2024 season. The league's rulebook defines the tackle as when a player bringing a runner to the ground "grabs the runner with one or both hands or wraps the runner with both arms" and "unweights himself by swiveling and dropping his hips and/or lower body, landing on and/or trapping the runner's leg(s) at or below the knee."

The play can result in a 15-yard penalty and a fine, which the NFL has issued 16 times so far this season. The New Orleans Saints' Vernon Broughton, for example, was fined $8,381 for what the NFL ruled was a hip-drop tackle in Week 10.

Fox Sports rules analyst Mike Pereira initially said during the Munich game broadcast Hutchinson's sack didn't qualify as a hip-drop tackle (h/t ESPN's Mike Reiss).

"Three things have to happen: you have to unweight yourself, swivel all around the back and land on the back of his leg below the knee," Pereira said, per Reiss. "This was more of a horse collar-type pulled down from behind... certainly not a horse collar penalty."

Hutchinson, who had recorded six sacks and six tackles for loss in nine games this season, will still pay a steep penalty as he begins recovering from an ACL tear and what Rapoport reported could also be additional damage to the meniscus in his right knee.

The Lions (7-2) will have to continue their pursuit of the top seed in the NFC without their best pass rusher, while the Patriots (5-5) will look to stay in contention long enough to give Maye a shot at returning to the lineup.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are set to face off against the Detroit Lions in Week 11 in what should be a hard matchup. Unfortunately for them, their quarterback is also fighting through an injury.

Quarterback Baker Mayfield suffered a foot injury against the Chicago Bears in Week 9. He was reportedly in doubt to play against the Bears, but after practicing on Thursday and Friday, it seems as if he will indeed start despite the injury.

The exact specifics of Mayfield's injury weren't known - until now. An NFL insider revealed those specifics on Saturday, and Mayfield's injury is among the more painful an athlete can suffer.

Baker Mayfield Dealing With Plantar Fascia Injury

NFL insider Tom Pelissero revealed that Mayfield is dealing with a plantar fascia injury. It's the connective tissue at the bottom of the foot that extends from the heel to the toes.

The injury is notably a very painful one. Per Pelissero, Mayfield will have to wear a special orthotic and new cleats to help manage the injury as he starts against the Lions on Sunday.

It isn't the first time the Bucs have had a player dealing with this injury in recent memory. Right tackle Luke Goedeke suffered a plantar fascia injury last season when he tore it in Week 2. He missed six games and spent seven weeks on injured reserve, returning to action that November.

It's unknown if Mayfield tore his plantar fascia or merely strained it. It is almost certainly not as severe as Goedeke's injury, but either way, Mayfield won't miss a game because of it, and he'll be back on the field just two weeks after suffering the injury against the Bears.

Mayfield is also dealing with a dislocated thumb he suffered in Week 3 against the Minnesota Vikings. He's still recovering from that injury, too, so he'll be pretty banged up heading into this matchup.

The Bucs will face the Lions at 1 p.m. on Sunday. It will be a tough task already, but with Mayfield playing through multiple injuries, it might get even harder.

text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Steelers have activated wide receiver Roman Wilson from injured reserve ahead of Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

Fellow wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr., though, was not activated from injured reserve. The Steelers will also be without outside linebacker Nick Herbig, who was downgraded to out with a hip/ribs injury Saturday.

The Steelers elevated practice squad wide receiver Max Hurleman after the former undrafted free agent earned votes of confidence from quarterback Aaron Rodgers and coach Mike McCarthy over the past two weeks. They also signed linebacker KJ Henry to the active roster to help replace Herbig.

Wilson has been out since fracturing one finger and dislocating another in the Steelers' Week 5 win against the Indianapolis Colts. His return figures to boost the Steelers' sluggish passing game and could help alleviate the attention on top receiver DK Metcalf, who has struggled throughout the season.

A 2024 third-round pick, Wilson was developing into a reliable deep threat prior to his injury, with touchdowns in back-to-back games for the first time in his career.

"Instead of having four receivers up, we'll probably have five or six," Metcalf said Thursday. "So I mean a lot more rotation, a lot of fresh bodies. But just watching them out there at practice these past couple days, they look fresh, they look ready to go to me."

Wilson had his 21-day practice window to return from injured reserve opened earlier this week and was a full participant in practice each day this week.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The best ability is availability. The Green Bay Packers kicked off their practice week on Saturday with all 52 players on the active roster going through drills on the practice field.

That doesn’t mean the Packers are completely healthy headed into their Wednesday night game at the Los Angeles Rams. However, seven players who either did not play against the Vikings last week or dropped out of the game were back on the field following their make-believe bye week.

Micah Parsons Practices Again

The list starts with star edge rusher Micah Parsons, who is entering his third week of practice. Presumably, he will be the 53rd player on the roster for the huge showdown against the Rams, with this week representing the finishing touches on his comeback from last year’s knee injury.

“I think we’ll have a better indication the closer we get to this thing,” coach Matt LaFleur said before Saturday’s practice. “Certainly, he’ll be out there and his ability to go out there and perform at practice will be the ultimate indicator.”

Josh Jacobs Returns

Running back Josh Jacobs was back after missing the Vikings game with a broken finger sustained a week earlier against New England. Jacobs will be able to play through the pain, but the key will be whether he will be able to play with critical ball-security while wearing a protective device following surgery..

“I’m not anticipating that [he will play against the Rams], but we’ll see how he progresses,” LaFleur said. “He would definitely have to prove the function in order to play.”

If Jacobs is out, Kaleb Johnson might be the team’s No. 1 back. After barely playing in two games and then not playing at all in two games due to a couple fumbles, Johnson has rushed for 110 yards the last two games. The rest of the team had 75 rushing yards.

“I think he’s grown, I think he’s learned a lot from the time he’s gotten here till now,” LaFleur said. “He’s done a better job in just owning his responsibilities and doing his one-eleventh. That’s encouraging.”

Change on Offensive Line?

The Packers have had six starting combinations on the offensive line this season. Is No. 7 on the way?

Center Sean Rhyan, who suffered an ankle injury on the opening series at Detroit and missed the last three games, returned to practice. He’d add a more physical and experienced presence than John Williams.

“He’s a guy that’s played a lot of ball,” LaFleur said. “That’s not to take anything away from the job John’s done; I think he’s done a really admirable job going in there, having never really played it before and done a pretty good job. But there’s a reason he’s the starter, right? And there’s a reason we brought him back because he’s played good ball for us, and I think that can help.”

Meanwhile, Kevin Zeitler, who would have started at right guard against Minnesota if not for a triceps injury sustained during the Thursday practice, was back at practice.

Zaire Franklin Returning at Linebacker

Starting linebacker and defensive captain Zaire Franklin, who missed the last four games with a shin injury sustained at practice before the Detroit game, returned to practice, as well. That was no surprise considering he went through a pregame warmup before the Minnesota game.

“Another guy that’s got to go through the week and we’ll see where he’s at at the end of this thing,” LaFleur said.

While Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper and even Nick Niemann did a nice job filling the void, Franklin’s experience and physicality will help the defense and allow Hopper and McDuffie to serve larger roles on special teams.

Three More Players Return

Cornerback Brandon Cisse (rib), receiver Bo Melton (quad) and receiver/returner Skyy Moore (ankle) dropped out of the Minnesota game. All three players were back at practice.

Cisse, of course, is the standout defensive back and a key part of a defense that ranks fourth in yards allowed per passing play and fifth in opponent passer rating. Moore’s impact as a returner was missed when he went on injured reserve with a high-ankle sprain. He returned against the Vikings but was injured on his third kickoff return.

If Moore is not ready, the team re-signed receiver Coleman Owen to the practice squad. Owen handled the punt-return duties when Moore was on IR.

While the Packers practiced on Saturday and it’s a Wednesday in their world, the NFL will have the teams publish injury reports on Sunday, Monday and Tuesday. While everyone practiced for Green Bay, there’s a lot to be determined before Tuesday’s injury report and Wednesday’s inactives list.

“We've got a lot of guys in that boat where they’ve got to prove it, prove function throughout the course of the week, and they’ve got to feel confident that they can go out there and get the job done,” LaFleur said.

Packers Injured Reserve

The Packers have a total of 13 players on injured reserve or the physically unable to perform list. Parsons is the only player whose return-to-play window has been opened. So, it’ll be at least another week before defensive tackles Jonathan Ford (calf) and Warren Brinson (groin) will be available.

LaFleur provided a non-answer answer when asked about edge player Collin Oliver, who was injured in the second preseason game at Denver and started the season on injured reserve with a return-to-play designation.

“He’s still progressing through and making progress,” LaFleur said.

text:
With the Eagles at 2-7 and preparing to face the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, it’s a perfect time to hop into the Cold Tub Time Machine — I just made that up, I think — and head back to April 23.

What if Makai Lemon didn’t slide down the draft board? What if the Eagles didn’t move ahead of the Steelers — who literally were calling Lemon — to select him?

What would the Eagles have done with their pick?

It’s an interesting thought experiment, given what the Steelers did after realizing they couldn’t draft Lemon. They took offensive tackle Max Iheanachor, who visited the Eagles and plays a position they needed, one that came more into focus four weeks into the season when Lane Johnson retired.

But here are some numbers to chew on as Markel Bell, the team’s third-round pick, prepares to make another start at right tackle.

Iheanachor’s pressure rate allowed is 7.83%, while Bell’s is 7.14%, according to Pro Football Focus. Even Monroe Freeling, who was mocked to the Eagles by some and was drafted 19th by Carolina, is having a rough start to his NFL career with a pressure rate of 8.47%. Only Blake Miller (6.23%), picked 17th, is having a better season in pass protection than Bell among the tackles picked in the area of where the Eagles did.

Caleb Lomu, who is a backup in New England, went seven picks after Iheanachor at No. 28, and then no tackle was selected until the Eagles drafted Bell 40 picks later.

Bell’s first season hasn’t been perfect, and the circumstances haven’t been ideal, but he’s playing just as well as his peers drafted two rounds earlier.

How would we all be viewing Iheanachor if he was the first-round pick? How would the Eagles? Would they still be entering the offseason wondering if they had the right tackle of the future in the building?

Howie Roseman has gotten a lot of flak for the last two draft classes, and deservedly shoulders blame for the lack of talent on the 2026 roster, but drafting isn’t an exact science, and the tackles from the most recent draft class clearly show that.

It’s unclear if Bell is the future at right tackle, but it’s not because the Eagles didn’t draft Johnson’s replacement in the first round.

What we’re saying about the Eagles

Here’s what our columnists are saying this week, including Mike Sielski, who wrote about the decision facing the Eagles at quarterback after this season, and Marcus Hayes, who wrote that tanking is for “nerds and losers.”

Sielski: “Jeffrey Lurie might replace Nick Sirianni, and people here will be curious about the next head coach, but they won’t be excited. When the home team is losing, no one is sticking around to watch the new guy call plays. Only a young, promising quarterback brings that kind of juice.” Read more.

Hayes: “Tanking is for losers. Tanking is for nerds. The Eagles are 2-7 coming out of their bye. The immediate future looks bleak. They are riding two consecutive unproductive drafts. Still, anyone who thinks the Eagles should try to lose as many of their remaining games on purpose likely falls into one of those categories: loser, nerd, or both.” Read more.

David Murphy: “If the Eagles see a Patrick Mahomes somewhere beyond the Mitch Trubiskys of this year’s class, they should and most likely will draft him. Otherwise, they should and will see this disaster of 2026 for what it is: A chance to make themselves significantly better at some other premium positions, and thus return Hurts to a position where he has shown he can succeed.” Read more.

What the Steelers are saying

It’s been a long time since the Steelers won a game in Philadelphia. Head coach Mike McCarthy offered his team a history lesson this week.

“[We] talked about 1965, and so we’re definitely aware of that,” McCarthy said. “Talked about the Steagles during World War II. Anytime there’s a history component, I think it’s important to recognize that with your players, especially your new players, that’s part of their experience here, and being in tune with the history and tradition of the Pittsburgh Steelers.”

Aaron Rodgers on Vic Fangio: “I have a ton of respect for him. He’s been in the league longer than me, and he’s had some incredible defenses. This is one of them. This is a really good defense. title: Kyle Shanahan confident in 49ers CBs bouncing back vs. Vikings: I 'know they'll be better'

text:
The San Francisco 49ers cornerbacks faced a mighty test against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 10 and failed.

They'll have another tough matchup in Mexico City against Justin Jefferson and the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, but coach Kyle Shanahan -- in part because of the group's improved health -- believes they'll rise to the occasion this time around.

"You don't give guys excuses for not playing their best, but I also love when guys are healthy enough to play," Shanahan said on NBC Sports Bay Area's 49ers Game Plan regarding corners such as Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green. "But they are hurting, so you know they're not going to be their best, but they still give us the best chance to win. And some people's 85 percent or 90 percent is better than some other people's 100 percent. So, yeah, they got to play better, and I know [Lenoir] struggled the most. ... But I also respect them for going out there."

Lenoir and Green, San Francisco's starting corners, both missed two practices last week and were questionable ahead of the 46-40 shootout win over Dallas. Lenoir, who was dealing with a foot injury, looked the most affected. Dak Prescott torched Lenoir, picking on him relentlessly to amass 10 completions for 134 yards and three touchdowns on the 16 targets that went the sixth-year corner's way, while Green was tending to a back injury and allowed five catches for 37 yards on six looks. The secondary gave up a season-high 343 passing yards overall.

As Shanahan mentioned, the performance must be better regardless of health, but the this week's practice has been promising in terms of a potential rebound.

Lenoir didn't show up on the injury report at all. Green was limited with his back issue on Wednesday before participating in full for consecutive days. Neither has a game designation.

"I think what helps them the most is -- I think they survived that week," Shanahan said. "They didn't take a step back injury-wise. They've already had two and a half good practices this week, and that's why I already know they'll be better on Sunday."

After failing to slow down CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens and Ryan Flournoy, San Francisco now faces a pass-catching unit comprised of Justin Jefferson, Myles Price, T.J. Hockenson and Jauan Jennings, who has been quiet in his first year with the Vikings but will be squaring off against the team he spent his first five seasons with in the NFL.

The most fear-inducing member of the bunch is, of course, Jefferson, a former Offensive Player of the Year, but Minnesota's entire offensive operation took a massive step forward through the acquisition of quarterback Kirk Cousins.

After averaging 18.3 points per game in their first eight games of the season, the Vikings hung 30 on the Packers in Cousins' first game back with the team as the offense went over 300 total yards for only the third time in 2026.

Given how good the Vikings defense is, ranked first in points allowed and second in yards allowed with a relentless pass rush, the 49ers cannot afford to let Minnesota's offensive playmakers get loose nearly as frequently as they did the Cowboys'.

"They just got to take the space away," Shanahan said. "When you're going against a good receiver, like Justin, I don't care how good you are at covering -- if he can get up and do all their freaky things with their freaky movement, very similar to George Pickens, good luck defending every angle of the cut.

"Those guys are too good at separating. So, we got to close that space, get on those guys fast and not give them as much room."

How well San Francisco does against the pass on Sunday Night Football could very well determine the game's outcome.

The cornerbacks atop their depth chart are healthier. Now, will they be better?

text:
The Arizona Cardinals are turning to their fourth quarterback of the season.

On Saturday, the team ruled out quarterback Carson Beck for Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Beck has been dealing with back spasms and did not practice on Friday. Head coach Mike LaFleur said that the team was preparing for Josh Johnson to be the team's starter for Week 11.

Beck, who is a rookie, was thrust into the role of starter after Gardner Minshew went on injured reserve with a torn UCL. The Cardinals' original starter, Jacoby Brissett, was traded to the Baltimore Ravens after being benched for Minshew mid-game the week before.

Beck had been listed as questionable on Friday's injury report.

LaFleur said that this is an issue that Beck has dealt with before, but wasn't able to provide a clear timeline for a return.

In the meantime, the 40-year-old Johnson, who was signed off the Cincinnati Bengals' practice squad after the Minshew injury, will step up for Sunday's matchup against the Chiefs. At 40 years, 191 days, Johnson will be the second-oldest non-specialist to appear in a game for the Cardinals behind only Jim Thorpe (41 years, 185 days old), according to the team.

The itinerant backup quarterback also has some history with LaFleur: Johnson and LaFleur's careers overlapped in 2021, when both were with the New York Jets (LaFleur was an offensive coordinator at the time). LaFleur had high praise for Johnson, noting some of the reasons he's been able to keep his career going this long.

"If it is Josh, I've called plays for him before, and had a really great experience calling plays for him," LaFleur said. "He is incredible in the quarterback room, he's incredible for the starters. He's incredible for young quarterbacks, in terms of the way he sees the game, his energy, his positivity, how he keeps it real. He's mature. And he can still sling it. … If that's the route that ends up happening, let's go."

Arizona is the 15th NFL franchise that Johnson has been a part of in his career, as the veteran quarterback has bounced between half of the teams in the league. Across 16 seasons, he has only started 11 games in his NFL career.

NFL Official Suggests Puka Nacua's Injury Changed Suspension Talks The NFL suspended Nacua on November 19 for violating its personal conduct policy.

text:
The Los Angeles Rams received one piece of good news amid the controversy surrounding Puka Nacua.

The star receiver won't have to miss additional games because of his three-game NFL suspension.

However, one league official believes his injury changed how the case unfolded.

The official told The Athletic's Jonathan Jones that Nacua likely would have challenged the punishment more aggressively had he been healthy.

"Puka would have fought harder had he not been hurt," the high-ranking official with an NFL team told Jones on Nov. 21. "IR gave everybody an out."

The remarks raise queries about whether Nacua's injury helped both sides settle a case that might otherwise have dragged on.

NFL Official Suggests Puka Nacua's Injury Changed Suspension Talks

The NFL suspended Nacua on November 19 for violating its personal conduct policy.

But Jones reported that the league initially sought a punishment longer than three games. Officials had communicated that position to Nacua and the NFL Players Association before the receiver landed on injured reserve.

The two sides ended up reaching a negotiated settlement, ending the disciplinary dispute without an appeal.

Nacua suffered MCL and PCL sprains, along with turf toe, during the Rams' November 8 victory over the Washington Commanders.

Los Angeles placed him on injured reserve four days later.

That designation requires a player to miss at least four games. Nacua can serve his three-game suspension during that absence, meaning the punishment won't extend his time away from the field.

Regardless, the suspension carries a financial penalty. Nacua will forfeit approximately $961,167 in salary.

The NFL's decision stems from allegations involving a woman who accused Nacua of biting her and making an antisemitic remark on New Year's Eve in 2025.

According to Jones, the NFL determined that Nacua bit the woman without her consent.

Nacua's attorney has denied the allegation involving an antisemitic remark and previously characterized the biting as horseplay. Nacua has not been criminally charged.

The official's comments suggest that the timing of Nacua's injury may have helped resolve a dispute over the length of his punishment.

Rams' Puka Nacua Faces Lengthy Recovery After Knee Surgery

Nacua's suspension came with another unusual detail.

The NFL reportedly didn't know that the receiver had already undergone potentially season-ending surgery when it announced the punishment.

Nacua had surgery on his MCL on November 17, two days before the league issued its decision.

Head coach Sean McVay confirmed the procedure on Nov. 20.

"Puka Nacua decided to get surgery on his MCL on Tuesday, so that'll be a couple months for him," McVay said.

The coach also indicated that Los Angeles should prepare to finish the regular season without its star receiver.

That leaves Nacua's immediate playing future uncertain, regardless of when the suspension expires.

The 25-year-old caught 70 passes for 715 yards and four touchdowns in seven appearances this season.

He is also approaching a major contract decision, with his rookie deal expiring after the 2026 campaign.

For now, the Rams have clarity on his punishment, as he recovery remains a looming question.

text:
Even though the Miami Dolphins listed center Aaron Brewer as questionable for their Week 11 game against the Buffalo Bills, all signs are pointing toward him being able to play Sunday.

Brewer took the final step toward getting out of the concussion protocol when he took part in a full practice Friday, and the only hurdle remaining will be reporting no symptoms Saturday.

It's a fair expectation then that Brewer will be back in the lineup after missing the game against the Indianapolis Colts.

The Dolphins did rule out two players Friday, punter Bradley Pinion and wide receiver Jared Wayne.

Replacing Wayne will be simple because veteran Jalen Tolbert again will be active. Fellow wide receivers Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell both were full participants in practice Friday and did not get a game status designation, meaning they're good to go.

Recent acquisition Jack Browning will do the punting after being signed to the practice squad this week, and it's probably fair to assume he'll simply be elevated for the game.

The Dolphins also will look to the practice squad for kicker Daniel Carlson and likely defensive tackle Matthew Butler, but with only two elevations allowed, one will have to be signed to the 53-man roster.

The Dolphins also could have to make room for cornerback Darrell Baker Jr., who was a full participant all week and appears ready to contribute on special teams.

It will make for another interesting Saturday of personnel moves.

The Dolphins listed two other players as doubtful, including starting safety Dante Trader Jr., but it's difficult to envision him playing after he didn't practice all week. Also listed as doubtful was cornerback Jaylin Simpson, who's dealing with a knee injury. He's mainly a special teams contributor and Baker might wind up taking his place.

The only other Dolphins player with a game status designation was cornerback Marcellas Dial Jr., who has been a healthy scratch in recent weeks.

The best projection if Trader indeed is out against Buffalo would be for Zayne Anderson to get the start alongside rookie Michael Taaffe even if Kyle Louis has been getting regular snaps on defense since coming off IR. Louis has been used as a type of nickel linebacker as opposed to a true safety.

BILLS INJURY UPDATE

Like the Dolphins, the Bills ruled out two players Friday and both happen to be starters on defense, cornerback Christian Benford and linebacker Dorian Williams

The Bills also have injury issues at tight end, which could impact to some degree their running game. Starter Dalton Kincaid was listed as doubtful after not practicing all week because of thumb and ankle issues, while Jackson Hawes was listed as questionable after being limited all week.

The Bills had two others listed as questionable, safety Damar Hamlin (toe) and defensive lineman T.J. Sanders (shoulder).

Starting cornerback Dee Alford cleared concussion protocol and will play.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have spent the past few weeks overcoming a slow start to the season, and while the NFC South is still very much up for grabs, this team needs to start winning games on a more consistent basis. For much of the week, though, it has appeared as if the team's starting quarterback, Baker Mayfield, would be out in Week 11 due to a foot injury.

Even with a bye week in Week 10, the overarching expectation a few days ago was that Mayfield's newest ailment would prevent him from playing in yet another game this season. And yet, Mayfield has appeared to make some substantial progress over the team's past few practice sessions, so much so that it appears he is now actually trending towards playing vs. the Detroit Lions on Sunday.

It's been an odd season for Mayfield and the Bucs offense, to say the least. While he's missed time with a thumb injury, even when he's been on the field, Mayfield hasn't been all that great for Tampa Bay. Through six games, he's completing just 60.6% of his passes for 922 yards, three touchdowns, and four interceptions.

Considering how the Buccaneers just handed Mayfield a three-year, $165 million contract extension before the start of the season, it's pretty clear that this isn't the sort of production the team was hoping for from him. Sure, injuries have prevented the offense from ever really having a shot to get off the ground, but Mayfield is being paid to be the guy who can win games on his own.

Instead, a new foot injury seemed set to force Mayfield to stay on the sidelines for another week, with undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels appearing to be set for another spot start. Instead, Mayfield has ramped up his activity at practice throughout the week, with NFL insider Jeremy Fowler of ESPN revealing that he seems to be on track to play in Week 11 now.

"I'm told he got a lot more reps Friday at practice, so he seems to be ramping up to play," Fowler said on "SportsCenter." "Head coach Todd Bowles put him through the paces on their turf field because they're going to be playing in Detroit, make sure that foot is no issue on a harder surface. So, seems to be trending in the right direction there."

Buccaneers Need Baker Mayfield to Deliver the Goods in Week 11

As the regular season unfolds, games begin to get more and more important, and we are starting to reach that point of the year for the Bucs. A 3-6 record would seemingly disqualify them from being in the postseason hunt, but with the Carolina Panthers leading the division with a 4-5 record, a playoff push is still very much in the cards for this team.

In order to have any shot at accomplishing that, though, Mayfield is going to have to begin playing like the version of himself that Tampa Bay was hoping to receive when it gave him his aforementioned contract. In order to beat the Lions, the Buccaneers are going to have to put up points on offense, so if Mayfield plays, he's going to need to turn in his best outing of the season if he wants to have a shot at leading his team to victory.

title: Fantasy Football Week 11 injuries: T.J. Hockenson returns, Walker ruled out - CBS Sports
description:
We are projecting Bowers to play this week, which of course makes him a must-start tight end.
You may want to pick up Michael Mayer just in case, as Mayer would be a borderline top 12 tight end if Bowers is ultimately unable to go.
We'll view Waller as a borderline top-12 tight end if he is active.
With Hockenson back, we will rank him as a top 12 tight end.
Dalton Kincaid doubtful The tight end position looks even more like a disaster with Kincaid likely out.
text:
With six teams on a bye, we really needed more guys to come back in Week 11. Early reports suggest that may be the case. The big question, especially for guys who have been out for a while, is whether they will come back 100% to their former role. There are two lines of thought when it comes to guys who have been out for a while. One, they have fresh legs. Two, they need to shake the rust off or work their way back. On Thursday, we saw what looked like fresh legs as David Montgomery had his best rushing game of the season in his return. Hopefully we see more performances like that the rest of the weekend.

Kenneth Walker ruled out

The Chiefs are huge favorites against the Cardinals and play the Bills on Thanksgiving, so it makes sense to give Walker another week. Emmett Johnson is once again a must-start running back and my number two running back overall in full PPR leagues.

Brock Bowers was present at practice on Thursday

We don't think this was a full practice, but it is fantastic news that he was there at all after leaving Week 10 with an ankle injury. We are projecting Bowers to play this week, which of course makes him a must-start tight end. You may want to pick up Michael Mayer just in case, as Mayer would be a borderline top 12 tight end if Bowers is ultimately unable to go.

Baker Mayfield returned to practice on Thursday

Mayfield missed Wednesday but got a limited session in on Thursday. While the vibe early in the week was negative, we're now prepared to project Mayfield as in on Sunday. That doesn't mean we want to start him. What it does mean is that Bucky Irving is a must-start RB1, and Emeka Egbuka is an upside WR3. Still, if you picked up Jalon Daniels in a Superflex league, you should hold him just in case.

DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks trending towards return

Smith and Wicks were both at practice on Wednesday and Smith sounds like someone who will play. If he does, he's the only Eagles wide receiver we want to start, and he'll be ranked as a WR2. If Smith needs one more week, then Makai Lemon is in play as a borderline WR2 in full PPR. Joe Milton is still expected to start at quarterback, so we won't get too excited about anyone in this passing game. For what it's worth, we like Dallas Goedert more without Smith than with him, but he's a top 12 tight end either way.

Darren Waller and Tommy Tremble both questionable

Waller and Tremble both got limited sessions in on Thursday and Friday. Since Week 8, Bryce Young has thrown 34.7% of his passes to tight ends, so either of these could be used in a pinch. We'll view Waller as a borderline top-12 tight end if he is active. If Waller is out, then Tremble is a high-end TE2. If either misses, it could be a boost to Jalen Coker, who has seen his target share shrink as the tight ends got more involved. Jonathon Brooks is also questionable, but we don't expect him to have a meaningful role even if he's active.

Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman questionable

The biggest impact here is a big blow to Germie Bernard, who falls outside of the top 40 receivers. We are ranking Wilson as a low-end WR3 and DK Metcalf as a borderline WR2. If the Steelers have success running the ball against Philadelphia, it may turn out that you do not want to start any of the Steelers' pass catchers. We would like to see Pittman do something positive before we even think about putting him in our lineup.

Jordan Addison out, T.J. Hockenson and Jauan Jennings back

Addison had surgery on his thumb. He won't go on IR, but he definitely won't play this week. That could make Jennings more interesting in a revenge game, but Jennings has shown nothing this year that would make you want to trust him. With Hockenson back, we will rank him as a top 12 tight end. This is a small boost for Kirk Cousins, who is a low-floor streamer.

Geno Smith attempting to play, Omar Cooper and Isaiah Williams out

I am not sure Smith will get in a full session this week but he has said he plans to play through his ankle injury. We don't really want to start him, but would much rather start Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall if he plays. Adonai Mitchell is also a good boom/bust WR3 assuming Smith plays. Mitchell gets a boost with the decrease. If Cade Klubnik has to start, we will downgrade the entire Jets offense.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt practicing in full

We are expecting Croskey-Merritt to return on Monday night but we have no idea how touches will be distributed between him, Rachaad White, and Austin Ekeler. Unless you are in a truly desperate situation, we would like to avoid all three. If you must, we are ranking them White, Crockey-Merritt, and Ekeler in that order. The first two are high-end flexes while Ekeler is only for the most desperate of managers.

Dalton Kincaid doubtful

The tight end position looks even more like a disaster with Kincaid likely out. Dawson Knox could be a deep steamer at the position, but we don't have much faith in him, especially since the Bills are huge favorites and may not throw many passes. This could be a small boost in targets for Khalil Shakir, who is a low-end WR3.

Josh Johnson preparing to start for Carson Beck

The Arizona Cardinals nightmare continues. While it is never a good thing to start your fourth different QB, I am not sure there will be a huge drop-off from what Beck was going to give us. You can be as nervous as you want about Trey McBride; there's no sitting him. We don't really want to start anyone else from this offense but Zonovan Knight is our favorite flex if you are absolutely desperate.

Mike Evans trending towards questionable

The 49ers have a huge game this week against the Vikings, so it wouldn't be surprising if Evans pushes to play. How much he plays is another question altogether. I think the safest way to view Evans is as an upside WR3 if he gives it ago. We would be much less interested in starting Keenan Allen and Deebo Samuel if Evans returns. What's worse is this is a Sunday night game, so you'll need a backup plan if you are waiting out any of these guys.

Ladd McConkey limited

title: Hutch should take a page from Barry Sanders, avoid injury | Letters - Detroit Free Press
description:
I have been a Detroit Lions fan since the early 1960s, and I have seen the NFL change for the good and for the not so good.
In the words of Bo Schembechler, "The Team, The Team, The Team!"
When we finally got a television, one of the two channels carried the Lions' Thanksgiving Day game.
I am an unapologetic, loud, proud Bills fan, but for a couple of hours on Thanksgiving Day, I will be a loud proud Lions fan.
("Mitch Albom: Laughing at Kirk's murder only shows how low we have sunk," Detroit Free Press, Nov.
text:
Hutch, we needed you on the field

I grew up watching the Lions on black and white TV in the days of Milt Plum, Lem Barney, Joe Schmidt, Dick "Night Train" Lane and Tommy Watkins.

I have been a Detroit Lions fan since the early 1960s, and I have seen the NFL change for the good and for the not so good. The thing that bothers me greatly is how today's players make everything about them, not the team.

In this modern era of the NFL, there is one player who was the consummate pro in how he conducted himself on the field of play, and that was Barry Sanders.

After one of his spectacular runs or touchdowns, he didn't run and chest bump a teammate, he didn't spike the ball, he didn't run and jump into the stands, he just handed the ball to the referee.

I'm saying all of this to address Aidan Hutchinson's injury, that was avoidable! He wasn't hurt on a play, he was hurt celebrating a sack, something he gets paid to do, something he is supposed to do. Because of his actions, he is lost for the season as the Lions make a playoff run, and his season is over.

More importantly, he has let his team down. As a star player at his position, he needs to understand his importance to the team and act accordingly. Today's players make what they do about them, look at me, see what I did. Just do your job and let that speak for itself, like Barry did. High five a teammate, don't put more stress on your body than the game already does. I recall some years ago another Lion did the same thing and was lost for the season due to injury.

Hutch, we need you on the field, not on crutches. In the words of Bo Schembechler, "The Team, The Team, The Team!"

James J. Smith

Battle Creek

Bills fan will root for Lions on Thanksgiving Day

During the war, my father was stationed at Selfridge Field. The Detroit Lions let military attend games for free. My father would buy a ticket for my mother, take her to her seat, go to the seats allotted to the military, and after the game started, go and sit with my mother.

I was born after the war, and can remember not having a television as a child. When we finally got a television, one of the two channels carried the Lions' Thanksgiving Day game. Since that game, I have missed only one game.

In 1969, I was in basic training, and while there was no training scheduled on Thanksgiving Day, I was caught reading a newspaper and was given extra duty, and I missed that game.

The first time I saw the Lions play live was the last game played at War Memorial Stadium in Buffalo. It was a 21-21 tie. The next year, the Bills moved into the Ralph. I am an unapologetic, loud, proud Bills fan, but for a couple of hours on Thanksgiving Day, I will be a loud proud Lions fan.

Let’s go, Lions.

Theodore E. Boesel

Rochester, New York

Dan Campbell is to blame for Lions discipline problems

The Detroit Lions have chronic team discipline problems, and the responsibility for it sits with the coach.

I have a hard time believing Brad Holmes, when he drafted this team, had the foresight to see some of the incredible, non-football nonsense that happens in these games. And the referees see it.

How many penalties will it take before one finally sees the same old, same old Lions?

Dan Holden

Essexville, Michigan

There's a long history of Black cowboys

Jordan Williams follows a long tradition of Black cowboys and lawmen in both history and local popular culture. ("Why did 2 horses board a Detroit bus? See footage, hear from owner," Detroit Free Press, Nov. 13.)

The number of Black U.S. deputy marshals sworn by Judge Isaac Parker to serve in Indian Territory was disproportionate to numbers in the regional population, and one such deputy marshal, Bass Reeves, was most probably the model for The Lone Ranger, which originated on Detroit radio station WXYZ in 1933.

Harry Frank

Ann Arbor

Albom's selective outrage at cruel humor

Mitch Albom is right. Laughing at someone's murder is not funny. ("Mitch Albom: Laughing at Kirk's murder only shows how low we have sunk," Detroit Free Press, Nov. 15.)

I do not recall reading a similar editorial when the president himself mocked a brutal attack on Paul Pelosi, and when his son created a meme about a Halloween costume mocking the Pelosi attack. That was not funny either.

Also not funny was slamming Robert Mueller's death, slamming John McCain's capture, and so much more that comes out of the White House.

Let's put the blame for lowered standards where it belongs.

Mocking a disabled reporter in 2015 should have derailed Donald Trump's election immediately, Instead, it started the country down a path of cruelty as humor.

The president is supposed to set an example. What does one expect as the American people follow the example of the grotesque and cruel "humor" constantly demonstrated by the leader of the country? You reap what you sow.

Roxanne Lopetrone

Garden City

The RenCen plans look great

I, my wife and my children were born in Detroit. I'm retired, but my international law firm is still headquartered in Detroit. I lived in Detroit for much of my career. I am 85, and have been a Detroit fan longer than many of the critics of the RenCen deal outlined by the recent Jamaine Dickens editorial have been alive. ("The RenCen deal costs Detroiters nothing. Rejecting it will," Detroit Free Press, Nov. 11.)

I have watched with dismay the negative attitudes of the harsh critics of the proposal to open up a plaza on the Detroit River and rehab the RenCen. Frankly, the plans look great and this project will save one of the most dominant features on the Detroit skyline from becoming a symbol of decay and decline. It is incredible that it is being criticized by people who have no money on the line. I am reminded of many MAGAs: "I'll believe what I want to believe; spare me the facts."

Despite my last name, I am (unfortunately) not related to him, and have never met the man. But in my view, he was one of the primary saviors of Detroit when it was an international symbol of urban decay. I lived and worked in Detroit during those times, and have a memory. It is appalling that, according to Dickens, he has some vociferous critics now.

Bob Gilbert

Leland

title: Patriots' Drake Maye Draws Concern From NFL Scout Before Injury Confirmation
description:

An NFL scout assigned to cover them doesn't like what that has brought out of Drake Maye.
